turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell noted that the number was quite satisfactory, but asked if Mr Worthing was in the habit of inviting the company of ladies who were not of the first rank of society.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack was surprised by the question, but he assured Lady Bracknell that he would only associate with the most respectable ladies.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell was not impressed by Jack’s assurance, she told him curtly, and asked if he had any other relatives of note, besides the aforementioned Lady Bloxham.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he did not have any relatives of note, but he would do his best to make Lady Bracknell proud of him as a son-in-law.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell was unimpressed by Jack’s assurances, she told him curtly, and enquired about the circumstances of his birth, as that was often a matter of great importance in the formation of one’s character.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack was taken aback by the question, but he composed himself and explained politely that he was born in a handbag and left in the care of a clergyman in the cloakroom of a London railway station.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell raised an eyebrow at Jack’s explanation, telling him curtly that the circumstances of one’s birth were indeed a matter of great importance, but that such a peculiar manner of arrival was quite unheard of. She inquired further if Jack had any other relatives of note, or if he had ever considered the possibility of his parentage being something more conventional.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack explained that he did not have any other relatives of note to mention, but he assured Lady Bracknell that he would do everything in his power to meet her expectations.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell was not satisfied with Jack’s response, telling him that his origin was indeed a matter of great concern, and that a gentleman who is discovered to have been brought up under such circumstances was not to be trusted.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack felt his cheeks flush with embarrassment, but he managed a polite smile and assured Lady Bracknell that he would do his best to live up to her high standards.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: She dismissed his assurances with a wave of her hand, telling him that while she appreciated his efforts, the matter of his unusual birth was indeed a significant drawback. She inquired sternly if he had any substantial means or a respectable profession to recommend him.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack assured Lady Bracknell that he was a gentleman in every respect, despite the unusual circumstances of his birth. He told her that he had a respectable profession and substantial means to support a wife.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: She inquired sharply if Mr. Worthing had a substantial income and a reputable profession, for it was no use to her daughter to marry a man without either.

turns.speaker: Jack
turns.text: Jack was determined to prove himself, he told Lady Bracknell, and assured her that he had a reputable profession as a gentleman and substantial means to support a wife.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: She raised an eyebrow, telling Jack that while his profession as a gentleman was indeed respectable, it was not sufficient without substantial means. She inquired sharply about the nature of his income and whether it was derived from investments or other reputable means.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: Gwendolen was watching her mother's interrogation of Jack with growing frustration, she interjected, her voice reproachful, how could Mama be so heartless as to question Jack's worthiness when she herself was in love with him.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Gwendolen with a look of exasperation, telling her daughter that love may be a luxury but marriage was a serious business that required a foundation of financial stability and social standing.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: How could Mama be so unfeeling as to insist on financial stability before considering love, Gwendolen thought, Jack was everything to her, and she would not let his lack of wealth define their future together.

turns.speaker: Lady Bracknell
turns.text: Lady Bracknell turned to Gwendolen with a look of exasperation, telling her daughter that love may be a luxury but marriage was a serious business that required a foundation of financial stability and social standing.

turns.speaker: Gwendolen
turns.text: How can Mama think that money and status are more important than true love and happiness, she wondered, it was as if Mama did not understand the depth of her love for Jack.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell that she was engaged to Mr. Worthing, mamma.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen that she was not engaged to anyone and that when she did become engaged, she or her father would inform her of the fact.

opening.speaker: Gwendolen
opening.text: Gwendolen told Lady Bracknell, 'Mamma!'

opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Gwendolen to go to the carriage.

opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack to take a seat.

opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she felt bound to inform him that he was not down on her list of eligible young men.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he must admit he smoked.

opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she was glad to hear it and that a man should always have an occupation of some kind.

opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he was twenty-nine.

opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack if he knew everything or nothing.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he knew nothing.

opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she was pleased to hear it and that she did not approve of anything that tampers with natural ignorance.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that his income was between seven and eight thousand a year.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell asked Jack if his income was in land or in investments.

opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that his income was in investments.

opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that it was satisfactory.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he had a country house with some land attached to it, about fifteen hundred acres.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that a country house was satisfactory and asked how many bedrooms it had.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that he owned a house in Belgrave Square, but it was let by the year to Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Lady Bracknell
opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that she did not know Lady Bloxham.

opening.speaker: Jack
opening.text: Jack told Lady Bracknell that Lady Bloxham went about very little and was a lady considerably advanced in years.

opening.text: Lady Bracknell told Jack that nowadays that was no guarantee of respectability of character and asked what number in Belgrave Square.
